newsitem.title: USA: EDS shares plunge on disappointing earnings, outlook.
newsitem.headline: EDS shares plunge on disappointing earnings, outlook.

text.p: Electronic Data Systems Inc. stock plunged on Friday, losing nearly 15 percent of its value a day after the company posted the latest in a string of disappointing earnings.

Analysts rushed to downgrade the stock after the information services giant warned of weaker-than-expected results for the year, but advised investors against abandoning EDS as the company competes for a handful of lucrative multi-billion dollar contracts in the months ahead.
"(Investors) should go to the sidelines and wait for a sign to jump in again," Cowen & Co. analyst Hugh Shytle said.
Stock of Dallas-based EDS fell $6.25 to $36.81 in heavy trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active issue, with more than 8.4 million shares traded.

EDS, a leading global provider of information services, said Thursday that, excluding special charges, its net income in the second quarter fell to $192.4 million, or 39 cents a share, from $246.6 million, or 51 cents a share, a year earlier, also excluding charges.

Since revenues and earnings are expected to be eroded, mainly because of a small number of contracts booked before 1996, EDS anticipates 1997 earnings of $1.90 to $2 a share before any charge -- well below its earlier estimate of $2.30 to $2.35 a share.

Analysts said the trimmed earnings estimates may prove optimistic if the Plano, Texas-based company is unable to slow an erosion of revenues from former parent General Motors Corp. and cope with lower profit margins in the increasingly competitive information technology industry.
"We have only modest confidence in these estimates, pending a return to more normalcy," Merrill Lynch analyst Stephen McClellan said.
One key to EDS' outlook is its ability to win a so-called "mega-contract," industry jargon for the multi-billion dollar information technology outsourcing deals that have eluded the company of late.
EDS is competing for at least three such deals that could generate some forward momentum for a company that has posted disappointing earnings in three of the past four quarters.
The company reportedly is negotiating final terms of a $4 billion, multi-year pact to be principal supplier to BellSouth Corp.'s telecommunications unit in a deal expected to close in early December.

EDS also is on the short list for a $4.5 billion deal with Commonweath Bank of Australia, and is competing for a multi-billion dollar deal with the state of Connecticut, which is outsourcing its information technology operations and expected to announce a winner this autumn.
"I think the issue at EDS is there are mega-contracts out there, and they are going to win some of them and they are gonna lose some of them," Cowen & Co.'s Shytle said.
